market_context: United States and general English-speaking market
title: Oat milk vs. soy milk: nutrition differences

seo.title: Oat milk vs. soy milk: protein, calories and calcium
seo.meta_description: Compare current unsweetened oat and soy milks per cup for protein, calories, carbs, fiber, calcium and vitamin D.
seo.search_intent: Compare oat milk and soy milk nutrition

excerpt: Using current unsweetened products, Silk soy milk provides 8 g protein per cup while Oatly Unsweetened lists 0 g. Fortification can make calcium and vitamin D look similar despite very different macros.
content_html:
Oat milk and soy milk can occupy the same glass without doing the same nutritional job. In current U.S. unsweetened examples, Silk Unsweet Soymilk provides 8 g protein per cup while Oatly Unsweetened provides 0 g. Both are fortified, so calcium and vitamin D can look much more similar than the macronutrients.

One cup side by side

Silk Unsweet SoyOatly Unsweetened
Calories9040
Protein8 g0 g
Fat4.5 g1.5 g
Carbohydrate4 g6 g
Fiber2 g<1 g
Calcium470 mg320 mg
Vitamin D3 mcg4 mcg

The two drinks are similar in how people use them, not in protein. An 8 g gap in one cup is large enough to change breakfast meaningfully, especially if the beverage replaces dairy milk rather than simply lightening coffee.

Soy is much closer to milk as a protein source

Eight grams per cup puts this soy milk in the same general protein range as dairy milk. The Oatly example contributes none. Other oat milks may provide a few grams, so this is a comparison of two real products rather than a claim that every oat milk has zero protein.

Fortification can make micronutrients look surprisingly similar

Calcium and vitamin D in these beverages are largely added during manufacturing. Silk lists 470 mg calcium and 3 mcg vitamin D per cup; Oatly lists 320 mg calcium and 4 mcg vitamin D.

That is why the source ingredient alone does not tell you whether a plant beverage is a good calcium or vitamin-D source. Check the label, and shake the carton as directed because fortified minerals can settle.

Oat milk carries more carbohydrate in this comparison

The oat drink provides 6 g carbohydrate per cup versus 4 g in soy. Neither has added sugar in the products compared here, but “unsweetened” still does not mean carbohydrate-free.

Look beyond one nutrient if it replaces dairy regularly

Protein, calcium, vitamin D, vitamin B12, iodine, and potassium can all matter depending on the rest of the diet. Formulas vary substantially between brands and between original, barista, and unsweetened versions.

The practical choice

If protein is the priority, soy has a decisive advantage in these examples. Oat milk offers a different flavor and carbohydrate profile. For calcium and vitamin D, the comparison is about fortification, so the label on the exact carton matters more than the words “oat” or “soy.”

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: Soy by a wide margin in these examples: 8 g per cup versus 0 g.

faq.question: Can calcium be similar?
faq.answer: Yes when fortified, but amounts vary by product.

faq.question: Why does FDA emphasize soy?
faq.answer: Fortified soy beverages generally align more closely with milk's key nutrients.
